progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B5b: homologous pairs, one from each parent; crossing over swaps matching pieces between non-sister chromatids in prophase I; independent assortment at metaphase I; partners separate in meiosis I, so each gamete gets one of each pair; 2 to the power n, and 2 to the power 23 is more than 8 million; the plum and teal model cell with white letter beads. From B8: the four sources sorted into reshuffling and making new alleles; random fertilisation multiplies the combinations; siblings share alleles but differ; the deck of cards analogy (mutation prints a new card). From B9: a recessive allele shows only with two copies; a carrier has one; a letters-only Punnett square. From B4: a copying error that escapes repair is a mutation. From b01: a gene pool; a new allele starts as one copy in one individual; bacteria pass a mutation to both daughter cells. From b05: a mutation is inherited only if it is in the germ line. From B6a and b01: plasmids can carry genes between bacteria. Year 11: natural selection. Not assumed: ultimate against immediate source, the measured number of new mutations, the asexual limiting case.
progression.startsWith: Follow gamete formation and joining. The video opens: In 1977, a drought hit Daphne Major, a tiny island in the Galápagos.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the job of each process (mutation makes new alleles; meiosis shuffles existing alleles into varied gametes by crossing over and independent assortment; fertilisation joins gametes at random into new genotypes); tracing a new allele from a mutation in one gamete to a carrier with one copy in every cell, to half that carrier's gametes, to new combinations with other alleles, to offspring with one copy, and to offspring with two copies only when two carriers mate (one in four); explaining that in one generation almost all the differences between offspring come from reshuffling (about sixty to seventy new mutations per human child against more than eight million chromosome combinations per parent); explaining that every allele first arose by mutation, so mutation is the ultimate source and reshuffling the immediate one, and that without mutation no lost allele would be made again; explaining that bacteria reproduce asexually, without meiosis and fertilisation, so their new variation comes from mutation and gene transfer; applying this to an unseen new-allele trace and an unseen evaluate claim.
progression.nextLesson: how mutation, gene flow and genetic drift change the alleles of a whole population (route entry bio-m6-b08).

teaching.task: Each new generation is full of variation, so where does it come from, and how do meiosis and fertilisation share the work with mutation?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why half a carrier's gametes carry the new allele (meiosis I separates the partners, 3); why the allele ends up in many combinations (crossing over swaps pieces; each pair faces either way, 4); why two copies need two carriers (each parent gives one allele per gamete, 5); why a recessive allele stays hidden (it shows only with two copies, 5); why siblings differ mostly by reshuffling (millions of combinations against tens of new mutations, 6); why mutation is still essential (every allele first came from it; without it, losses are permanent, 7); why bacteria differ (no meiosis or fertilisation, 8). Visible case: one amber bead followed from a sperm to a "dd" box; the finches frame the start and the close. Video advantage: the amber trail persists across three scenes; the tallies tick against each other. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items with every given on screen. Reading load: about three text items besides bead letters; the 10a card is the densest frame and is the task itself.
teaching.conversationalApproach: The 1977 Daphne Major drought shows selection drawing on variation that was already there, so the question is where that variation comes from; three processes get three jobs (mutation makes, meiosis shuffles, fertilisation combines); one amber new allele is followed from the mutation that makes it into half the gametes, into new neighbours by crossing over and independent assortment, and into a genotype that never existed at fertilisation; a tally compares about 70 new mutations per child with more than 8 million chromosome combinations per parent; mutation is still the ultimate source because, without it, the set of alleles is fixed; bacteria, which reproduce asexually, vary by mutation and gene transfer. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, then the decision rule hands off to b08.
teaching.openingDecision: In 1977, a drought hit Daphne Major, a tiny island in the Galápagos. The small, soft seeds ran out, and most of the medium ground finches died. The survivors tended to have deeper beaks, strong enough to crack the big, hard seeds that were left. Beak depth is largely inherited, so their chicks hatched with deeper beaks on average, too. No new mutation was needed, because the variation in beaks was already there. So where does all the variation in each new generation come from?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is an apply-and-explain item on an unnamed animal: a new recessive allele n arises in one sperm, the resulting animal has one copy in every cell and mates with an animal with no copies; state the expected fraction of offspring that carry n, then explain how an animal with two copies could arise later. It tests segregation in meiosis I and random fertilisation acting on a new allele, with different numbers from scene 5 (scene 5 shows only the carrier by carrier cross). 10c is an evaluate item: "Meiosis and fertilisation produce almost all the genetic variation in each generation, so mutation is not important." It tests the per-generation against long-term judgement and needs a verdict. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, short working where needed, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: "investigate the causes of genetic variation relating to the processes of fertilisation, meiosis and mutation (ACSBL078)". The ledger marks it a depth-study or practical point; the learner modelling practical is bio-m5-p02 (Module 5), and this video claims no practical conduct. Inquiry question: "How does mutation introduce new alleles into a population?" Update the ledger row for B6-IQ1-05 when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: Three boards, one visual language (B5b's and B8's). (1) The island board (hook, scene 7): the painted finches (`m6-finch-slender-beak-v1.png`, `m6-finch-deep-beak-v1.png`) and a coded seed strip (small soft seeds, large hard seeds), with a coded beak-depth dot strip above the birds (one dot per bird, no axis numbers). (2) The allele board (scenes 3 to 5, 10b): B5b's model cell plate (`b5x-cell-dividing-nospindle-v1.png`) with B5b's chromosome plates (`b5x-chromosome-single-pink-v1.png` plum role, `b5x-chromosome-single-teal-v1.png`) and white letter beads; amber fill is reserved for the new allele (B8 and b01 rule: only a mutation bead is ever amber-filled), so the student can follow one bead through every step; the new allele's bead is amber, lettered "d", and its partner allele is a white "D". Crossing over and assortment reuse B5b's `CrossOver` (plate mask) and `TwoWays` coin flips unchanged, so the student recognises them. Gametes are small nospindle cell plates with one chromosome; the Punnett square is letters only, HSC style (two letters per box, no cells or birds inside). (3) The tally board (scenes 6 and 8): two coded tallies side by side ("new mutations per child" against "chromosome combinations per parent") with B5b's number ticker; bacteria as `b6a-bacterium-v1.png` and `m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png`. Real objects are painted: finches, seeds (new plate), gametes (`m6-egg-sperm-dish-v1.png`, `b3a-sperm-v1.png`, `b3a-egg-v1.png`), bacteria. Chromosomes follow B5b's HSC-style plates with coded beads, never letter-tile strips. No people: scene 6's human numbers sit beside gamete plates and a coded genome bar. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides bead letters; each tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The island board opens with the finches, seed strip and beak-depth dots; the three job chips light in turn as the allele board follows the amber bead through the model cell, crossing over, the coin flips and the letters-only Punnett square; the tally board takes over for one generation's numbers, shrinks for the ultimate source and clears for the bacteria; B8's deck returns for memory; each attempt clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the two-branch decision board and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
